item.title: Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
item.description: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information.

item.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
item.description: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task.

item.title: Software advance brings complex quantum simulations to standard computers
item.description: A major software advance could aid the creation of bigger, more reliable quantum computers, a study suggests. Researchers have developed an algorithm that enables off-the-shelf computers to run quantum simulations previously only possible using the world's most powerful supercomputers.

item.title: A tiny magnetic whirlpool could point to a new kind of ultra-efficient memory
item.description: Every time a computer stores or erases information, it uses energy. The amount is tiny for a single operation, but those operations happen billions of times every second. For decades, scientists have wondered just how little energy a memory device could use before reaching the fundamental theoretical limit set by the laws of physics. Now, researchers have shown that it is possible to come close.

item.title: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a new way to probe electrons' quantum geometry
item.description: Researchers at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and the University of Regensburg have developed a method for determining, using light, a quantum property of electrons that has hitherto been difficult to access. The focus is on what is known as Berry curvature—a quantity that describes certain geometric properties of the quantum mechanical states of electrons. item.title: Faster molecular simulations identify promising diamond defects for quantum computers and sensors
item.description: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole. The research was recently published in the journal ACS Central Science and has already garnered attention from other experts in the fiel

item.title: Quantum physicists trace a century of controlling spin
item.description: A concept from the field of quantum mechanics, spin is a property of particles that has no direct counterpart in everyday experience. Since the early 20th century, researchers have learned to manipulate it deliberately by means of precisely shaped electromagnetic pulses. This has resulted in two technologies that are widespread today: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is commonplace in hospitals, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR) is used to determine the structures of proteins and

item.title: Could consciousness be quantum?
item.description: A controversial idea linking quantum physics and consciousness is moving from speculation towards experiments that could finally put it to the test

item.title: Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence?
item.description: A mathematical mechanism enables AI models to process language at scale, undergirding the current AI revolution. Our columnist asks: Why is attention the key? The post Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Computational model guides lighting design to improve color discrimination in aging eyes
item.description: Researchers have developed a new computational model that accounts for the effects of aging on our eyes' ability to discriminate color. It could help guide lighting designs that make it easier for older adults to perceive colors while preserving the expected appearance for people with typical color vision.

item.title: New spectroscopy method enables direct comparisons of nuclear sizes across heavy elements
item.description: The size of a nucleus (nuclear charge radius) is an important physical quantity that reflects the arrangement of protons and neutrons within the nucleus. Particularly in deformed nuclei, such as those of rare-earth elements, examining changes in the charge radius can deepen our understanding of nuclear structure and nuclear deformation.

item.title: Storing memory on a chip with flowing water
item.description: Like the folds in crumpled sheets or the footprints on recently trodden sand, certain materials mark their histories. Now, Yale researchers show that networks of flowing water and other fluids can store their own memories—similar to how a computer chip does—an innovation that could steer robots and provide insight into some simple organisms. The results are published in Physical Review X.

item.title: Jamming the flow to enable memory in quantum materials
item.description: Understanding and controlling phase transitions are fundamental to physics and central to many technological revolutions. There is currently strong interest in materials with coupled structural and electronic phase transitions, where controlling the transition plasticity naturally yields built-in memory—a key step in emulating neurons and synapses for "neuromorphic" or brain-like computing technologies.

item.title: 诺奖颁给冰立方：“天马行空的想法，值得被支持几十年”
item.description: 2026年10月6日，冰立方中微子天文台（IceCube）项目发起人弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）获得诺贝尔物理学奖。

item.title: “冰立方”为何获得2026诺贝尔物理奖？现场对话诺奖评委
item.description: 1988年，弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）提出一个构想，利用南极深处的冰层探测来自宇宙的中微子。二十多年后，这一构想成为覆盖一立方公里冰层的冰立方（IceCube）中微子天文台。借助埋在冰中的光传感器，研究人员捕捉到了具有天体物理起源的高能中微子，为研究遥远宇宙中的高能过程提供了新的观测途径。

item.title: 95岁获诺奖的卡根，中国弟子眼中的老师与学者
item.description: “卡根告诉我，好的研究在于质量，而不在于数量。他提到，自己的课题组人数最多时也只有十人左右，很多时候还要更少。后来我经常向同事和学生讲起这件事。在我看来，他所追求的科研理念，就是做新的化学、不一样的化学、有引领性的化学。”

item.title: 95岁卡根终于等到诺奖，25年前法国部长曾为他写信抱不平
item.description: 10月7日，瑞典皇家科学院将2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予法国化学家亨利·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），表彰他们发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应和自催化现象。

item.title: 2026诺贝尔化学奖给了法国95岁学者和日本75岁学者，日本科学诺奖得主已有28位
item.description: 10月7日，2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予亨利·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），以表彰他们“发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应与自催化现象”。2001年，诺贝尔化学奖表彰不对称催化研究，获奖者为威廉·诺尔斯、野依良治和巴里·夏普莱斯。卡根未获奖，引发法国学界不满，时任法国科研部长致信诺贝尔基金会。《自然》当年报道了这场争议。25年后，95岁的卡根因不对称合成中另一项贡献终获诺奖。

item.title: New chip-scale gyroscope measures rotation with unprecedented sensitivity
item.description: Researchers have developed a chip-scale optical ring-laser gyroscope that can measure rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour. This record sensitivity, approaching Earth's rotation rate of 15 degrees per hour, could eventually be useful for precision navigation and orientation systems, particularly where GPS is unavailable.

item.title: New framework links magnetic phase boundaries to string-like defects in spin ice
item.description: A research team led by Haruki Watanabe, a professor in the Department of Physics and the Jockey Club Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), in collaboration with professor Yukitoshi Motome and graduate student Sena Watanabe from the University of Tokyo, has developed a unified theory that predicts when two states of matter are genuinely distinct and when they are actually the same.

item.title: Robotic 'time crystal' organizes itself into a single rhythm despite random disturbances
item.description: Scientists have developed a material that can grow and coordinate its own movement until the entire structure pulses in unison, paving the way for versatile robots that behave more like living systems.

item.title: Optical skyrmions can control the motion of magnetic skyrmions
item.description: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) are swirling patterns of magnetization that form inside certain magnetic materials. They can behave like actual particles in many ways, exhibiting a stable internal structure and distinct boundaries. Because they are extremely small and can be pushed around with relatively little energy, MSks are regarded as promising information carriers in emerging technologies, including low-power memories and logic circuits. However, a major goal in the field has been to find practi

item.title: 'Carpet' growth method yields long-sought 2D quantum material
item.description: For decades, physicists have sought a practical two-dimensional topological insulator: an ultrathin material whose interior blocks electricity but whose edges conduct it. In ordinary wires, electrons constantly bounce off imperfections, losing energy. But along the edges of a 2D topological insulator, electrons with opposite spins travel in opposite directions, like cars in one-way lanes, so they rarely scatter and lose energy.

item.title: 光遗传学终于获得诺奖
item.description: 2026年10月5日，诺贝尔大会宣布，2026年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖授予卡尔·戴瑟罗斯（Karl Deisseroth）、彼得·黑格曼（Peter Hegemann）和格奥尔格·纳格尔（Georg Nagel），以表彰他们“在光门控离子通道和光遗传学方面的发现”。

item.title: 杨振宁先生在石溪
item.description: 对于杨振宁，中国读者熟悉的，多是他2003年回到清华园之后的岁月；而从1966年至1999年在石溪的33年，是杨振宁一生中最长的一段任职。

item.title: 诺奖得主格拉肖忆杨振宁：“我依然认为他是天才”
item.description: 诺奖得主格拉肖眼中的杨振宁：敢发表“错”论文的天才。

item.title: 尼安德特人和丹尼索瓦人算不算智人?
item.description: 尼安德特人、丹尼索瓦人与现代人的祖先之间存在真实的基因交流，并留下了可育后代。但这究竟意味着他们属于同一物种，还是只是边界模糊的近亲？科学家们给出了截然不同的答案。

item.title: 对话诺奖评委邹晓冬：化学奖为何三次盯上“手性”；中国已有诺奖级工作
item.description: 10月7日，2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予亨利·卡根（Henri Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），以表彰他们“发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应与自催化现象”。

item.title: Silicon qubits surpass 99.99% gate fidelity while operating three at once
item.description: Silicon spin qubits are a promising platform for building scalable quantum computers as they are compatible with the semiconductor manufacturing technologies used to produce today's computer chips. However, they have an important weakness: silicon spin qubits typically lose accuracy when several qubits are under parallel control. To be useful, quantum computers will need to operate many qubits simultaneously without compromising the accuracy of their operations.

item.title: Quantum sensor could measure how Earth drags spacetime
item.description: Einstein's theory of general relativity describes gravity as the bending of spacetime, a mathematical model that combines three-dimensional space and time into a single, four-dimensional continuum. The theory also predicts that a rotating object, such as Earth, slightly drags the surrounding spacetime as it rotates, a phenomenon known as frame-dragging.
